title: PESTLE: scanning the project environment
blurb: Describe why a project manager uses PESTLE, and sort external factors into the right category.
question: Harbourside Energy is starting a project to build an offshore wind farm. Before writing the business case, the project manager runs a PESTLE analysis. Why would she do this, and what kinds of factor would it uncover?

teach.h: Projects don't happen in a vacuum
teach.body: Plenty of things outside a project can knock it off course: a change of government, a recession, a new law, a breakthrough technology, local opposition, a storm season. None of them is under the project's control, but all of them can affect it. PESTLE is a simple checklist that helps a project manager scan that external environment systematically, so nothing big is missed.

letters.sub: Inflation, interest and exchange rates, recession
New, emerging or ageing technology, cyber threats
Laws and regulations, e.g. health and safety, data

teach.caption: Same letters, same order every time: Political, Economic, Sociological, Technological, Legal, Environmental.

teach.h: Why a project manager uses PESTLE
teach.body: PESTLE helps the project manager identify and assess the EXTERNAL factors in the project's environment that may affect it, so they can be managed rather than come as a surprise. The findings feed risk identification (threats and opportunities), stakeholder analysis, the business case and planning. It is used early, in concept and definition, and revisited as the environment changes.

head: Factor
Example
Could affect
rows: Steel prices and interest rates rise
Coastal residents object to the view
Bird migration routes and winter storms
teach.caption: Notice the technological factor is good news. PESTLE surfaces opportunities as well as threats.

steps.label: Scan
steps.sub: Work through each of the six headings

steps.label: List factors
steps.sub: What outside the project could affect it?

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: How likely, how big, how soon?

steps.label: Feed in
steps.sub: Risk register, stakeholder analysis, business case, plans

head: Pair
First is about…
Second is about…
rows: Laws and regulations that must be obeyed
teach.caption: A rule of thumb: if it is already law, it is Legal. If it is a policy, a promise or an election, it is Political.

teach.text: PESTLE helps you IDENTIFY external factors so they can be managed. It does not 'mitigate all risks', 'control technological change', break the work down or describe team roles: all classic distractors. And it looks outward: low team morale or a missing skill in your own team is internal, not a PESTLE factor.

rows.label: A general election is called for next spring
The pound falls, so imported parts cost more
Younger customers prefer to order by app
A new data protection regulation takes effect
The site sits on a flood plain

items.label: First scan
items.sub: Shapes the outline business case and feasibility

items.label: Deeper analysis
items.sub: Feeds the risk register, stakeholder analysis and plans

items.label: Revisit
items.sub: Has anything changed outside the project?

items.label: Check the context
items.sub: Will the outside world help or hinder adoption?

teach.caption: PESTLE is not a one-off form: the environment keeps moving, so the analysis is revisited.
SWOT also looks inward (strengths and weaknesses). PESTLE looks only at the external environment.

items: PESTLE: Political, Economic, Sociological, Technological, Legal, Environmental.
A project manager uses it to identify and assess the external factors that may affect the project.
Findings feed risk identification, stakeholder analysis, the business case and planning.
Use it early and revisit it. It cannot mitigate all risks, and internal team matters are not PESTLE factors.

summary: You can now describe why a project manager uses PESTLE: to identify and assess the external political, economic, sociological, technological, legal and environmental factors that may affect a project, feeding risk, stakeholder analysis, the business case and planning. You can also sort a factor into the right category and spot the classic distractors.

A.q: In a PESTLE analysis, what does the letter S stand for?
A.why: S stands for Sociological (often called Social): attitudes, demographics, culture and lifestyle.

whyNot.0: Strategy is not one of the PESTLE headings.
whyNot.2: Scope is defined inside the project; PESTLE looks at the external environment.
whyNot.3: Stakeholders are analysed separately, although PESTLE findings can inform that analysis.

A.q: What is the main reason a project manager uses a PESTLE analysis?
options: To identify external factors that could affect it
To break the project's work into manageable packages
To agree which team member will carry out each task
To remove every risk before the deployment starts
A.why: PESTLE is used to identify and assess the external factors in the project's environment that may affect it.

whyNot.1: Breaking down the work is done with a work breakdown structure.
whyNot.2: Allocating tasks to people uses a responsibility assignment matrix.
whyNot.3: No analysis can remove every risk; PESTLE helps identify factors so they can be managed.

A.q: The pound weakens sharply, making a project's imported equipment more expensive. Which PESTLE category does this fall under?
A.why: Exchange rates are an economic factor, and here they directly raise the project's costs.

whyNot.0: Political factors concern government policy and elections, not currency movements.
whyNot.1: Legal factors are laws and regulations; no law has changed.
whyNot.2: The equipment itself is unchanged; only its price has moved.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following could be identified in a PESTLE analysis?
1) A forthcoming general election
2) A shortage of skills in the project team
3) Stricter emissions regulations
4) A new competing technology
B.why: An election (1, Political), stricter emissions rules (3, Legal) and a competing technology (4, Technological) are all external factors.

whyNot.0: Item 2 is a skills gap inside the project team: an internal matter, not a PESTLE factor.
whyNot.1: Item 2 is internal, so any option including it is wrong.
whyNot.3: Item 2 is internal, and the election (1) is missing although it is a political factor.

B.q: Foundations for a mountain visitor centre are due to be laid in January, when heavy snow is common. Which PESTLE category does this relate to?
B.why: Weather and climate conditions at the site are environmental factors.

whyNot.0: Economic factors are things like inflation and interest rates.
whyNot.2: Technological factors concern new or ageing technology.
whyNot.3: Sociological factors concern people's attitudes, demographics and culture.

B.q: When is a PESTLE analysis typically first carried out on a project?
options: Only after handover, as a lesson learned
Once deployment is complete, for audit
Only when an issue has been escalated
B.why: PESTLE is used early, to shape the business case, risks and plans, and then revisited as the environment changes.

whyNot.0: By handover it is too late to plan for the factors it would have revealed.
whyNot.1: After deployment, the project has already been exposed to the external factors.
whyNot.2: PESTLE is proactive; waiting for an issue misses the point of scanning ahead.

C.q: A project manager says: 'Now we have done our PESTLE analysis, all the project's risks are mitigated.' What is wrong with this?
options: PESTLE identifies factors; it does not remove risk
PESTLE looks only at internal factors, not at risks
PESTLE is only ever used at the end of a project
PESTLE is a tool for allocating the team's roles
C.why: PESTLE helps identify and assess external factors. Those must then be managed through risk responses; no tool mitigates all risk.

whyNot.1: PESTLE looks at EXTERNAL factors, and these often become identified risks.
whyNot.2: PESTLE is used early and revisited, not only at the end.
whyNot.3: Team roles are not part of PESTLE; that is a classic distractor.

C.q: During deployment of a new rail line, the government announces a review of all transport funding. What should the project manager do?
options: Ignore it, as the PESTLE was done at the very start
Treat it as a technological change to control
Revisit the PESTLE and assess the political risk
Record it only in the lessons-learned report
C.why: The environment has changed, so the PESTLE should be revisited and the new political factor assessed and fed into risk management.

whyNot.0: PESTLE is revisited as the environment changes; it is not a one-off exercise.
whyNot.1: A funding review is political, not technological, and the project cannot control it.
whyNot.3: Waiting for lessons learned would leave a live threat unmanaged.

C.q: How does a PESTLE analysis most directly support risk management?
options: It sets the probability and impact score of each risk
It helps identify external threats and opportunities
It assigns a named owner to every project risk
It decides which risk response should be chosen
C.why: PESTLE is an identification technique: it surfaces external threats and opportunities to record and then analyse.

whyNot.0: Scoring probability and impact happens in risk analysis, after identification.
whyNot.2: Assigning risk owners is part of planning the response.
whyNot.3: Choosing a response comes after the risk has been identified and analysed.

reteach.title: Planning a summer street party
reteach.question: You are organising a street party for your road in August. What could happen OUTSIDE your control that might spoil it, and how does PESTLE help you think of everything?

blocks.body: Instead of worrying at random, you check each heading in turn. The council's policy on road closures (Political). The rising cost of hiring a gazebo (Economic). Half the street being away in the school holidays (Sociological). A neighbour's new speaker system (Technological). The road closure order and music licence (Legal). The British summer weather (Environmental).

blocks.text: Your volunteers falling out with each other is a real risk, but it is internal. PESTLE only covers the world outside the project.

explain.body: Political, Economic, Sociological (Social), Technological, Legal, Environmental. Learn them in order: exam options often swap in look-alikes such as 'Strategic', 'Ethical' or 'Ecological'.

test.q: Which list gives the PESTLE factors correctly and in order?
options: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental
Political, Ethical, Sociological, Technical, Legal, Economic
People, Economic, Social, Technological, Logistical, Environmental
Planning, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Ecological
test.why: PESTLE is Political, Economic, Sociological (Social), Technological, Legal, Environmental.

whyNot.1: Ethical is not a PESTLE heading, and Environmental is missing.
whyNot.2: People and Logistical are not PESTLE headings; P is Political and L is Legal.
whyNot.3: P is Political, not Planning, and E is Environmental, not Ecological.

explain.body: PESTLE scans the external environment: forces the project cannot control but must respond to. Internal matters such as team morale, missing skills or the project's own plan are handled by other tools.

test.q: Which of these would NOT appear in a PESTLE analysis?
options: A forecast rise in national interest rates
Low morale within the project team
test.why: Team morale is internal to the project. PESTLE looks only at external factors.

whyNot.0: Interest rates are an external economic factor.
whyNot.1: Planning regulations are an external legal factor.
whyNot.3: Public opposition is an external sociological factor.

explain.body: Political covers government policy, elections and political stability: decisions and intentions. Legal covers laws and regulations that are in force or coming into force: things you must comply with.

test.q: The ruling party announces a new policy of moving funding away from road building. For a bypass project, which PESTLE category does this fit best?
test.why: A change in government policy and priorities is a political factor.

whyNot.0: No law or regulation has been passed; this is a policy announcement.
whyNot.1: It may have economic consequences, but its source is a political decision.
whyNot.2: Nothing about the technology has changed.

explain.body: PESTLE is a means to an end. Its findings go into the risk register (as threats and opportunities), the stakeholder analysis, the business case and the plans, and the analysis is revisited as things change.

test.q: Which of the following does a PESTLE analysis typically feed into?
test.why: External factors found by PESTLE are recorded as risks (threats and opportunities) in the risk register.

whyNot.1: Timesheets record hours worked; they have nothing to do with external factors.
whyNot.2: Office layout is not informed by a PESTLE analysis.
whyNot.3: Payroll is a business-as-usual system, unrelated to PESTLE.
